title: What Experts on Kids' Social and Emotional Health Are Overlooking
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler responds to the pandemic-era push to put social and emotional well-being first in schools by arguing that experts overlook a major source of emotional harm, the ordinary curriculum and instruction. She urges caution about SEL programs and about nudging children to talk about trauma, noting that many students were not harmed and that some benefit more from absorbing tasks such as history or math. Her central claim is that ineffective reading instruction leaves many children unable to decode or lacking the academic knowledge to understand text, and that this makes them feel like failures every day. She uses psychologist Sheila Clonan's swimming-pool analogy and her own classroom observations to show the emotional toll. Her fix is to teach decoding effectively, build knowledge from kindergarten through a coherent curriculum, use writing to absorb content, and prefer explicit instruction to inquiry for novices. She reports that struggling students blossom most under knowledge-building curricula.
points: Wexler's thesis is that standard curriculum and instruction, not just the pandemic, routinely damage students emotionally by making them feel like failures.
She cautions that repeatedly nudging children to talk about trauma can mislead or harm, and that 60 to 70 percent of students were not negatively affected during the pandemic.
Clonan's swimming analogy captures the daily experience of a child who never receives effective decoding instruction.
Academic success is a key component of well-being, so experts using measures like Duckworth's Student Thriving Index should ask how many students answer no and why.
Teachers moving to knowledge-building curricula report that previously low-performing students gain the most confidence.
quotes: Encouraging kids to talk about trauma isn’t always helpful. If children didn’t have traumatic experiences, being repeatedly “nudged” to open up may make them feel they should have—or even lead them to falsely believe they did.

Not all children suffered during the pandemic. One panel of experts has estimated that 30 to 40% of students experienced negative impacts on their mental or social-emotional health during the pandemic. That’s troubling, but it also suggests that as many as 60 to 70% did not.

Standard approaches to curriculum and teaching have long been causing emotional damage to many students. That’s not the fault of individual teachers. As I’ve discussed before, it’s a systemic problem grounded in the divergence between teacher training and instructional materials on the one hand and scientific evidence about how learning works on the other.
And that’s what you’re doing for six and a half hours a day,” Clonan said. “Imagine what that does to your soul. So of course we’re seeing anxiety, frustration, depression sometimes.

I’ve also seen older students become defensive or resentful when they’re assigned books clearly meant for younger children, or when an adult expresses surprise that they don’t have basic information about the world that’s assumed by their textbooks. With the best of intentions, we’ve been making students feel like they’re failures, when in fact the system has failed them.
What these experts may not know is how many students would answer that question in the negative—and why. If they did, surely they’d be sounding the alarm.

Teachers who have switched to a knowledge-building curriculum frequently talk about how students who were previously categorized as low-performing—the ones in the bottom reading groups, the ones diagnosed with learning disabilities, the ones still learning English—blossom the most. And when they’re given access to the same content as their classmates and contribute insightful comments to class discussion, as they often do, these children gain self-confidence. They see themselves differently—and so do their teachers and their peers.
